So I'd like to return to a question that we presented in phase one, what is an OCP with an OCP is a statutory or legal document that guides the physical environmental, economic, social and cultural development of the city and provides a comprehensive policy framework to shape long term growth.
The adoption of an OCP is mandated by the province through the Planning and Development Act and it grants the city the authority to undertake planning initiatives.
The OCP is meant to be the overarching document that all other management documents align with.
And management documents include bylaws, policies, strategies, plans, procedures and guidelines.
Management documents most pertinent to this committee include the Heritage Plan and the Civic Heritage Policy.
So the city has made a commitment to reconciliation and has reflected this commitment in the OCP both in its writing and design process.
The OCP opens with a recognition of the city's location on Treaty 6 territory, where first nation and many people have occupied land since time immorial.
Along with a circular table of contents shown on this slide.

Presenting the OCP as a cycle represents a commitment to the goal of enhancing and honoring relationships with the original stewards of this land and brings an indigenous lens that emphasizes that no one section is more important than the others.
Section B, our local context provides an overview and local context of the Saskatoon area, including information on the city's location.
A history of the area and its inhabitants and details on the city's population, economy and land use.
This is a new narrative piece for our OCP, but its inclusion follows best practices from across Canada.
It acknowledges that your history of the Saskatoon area and the impacts of what Canada's colonial history has had on local indigenous people and communities.
To ensure the content of the OCP's accurate and representative, we put together a team of city staff, both indigenous and non-indigenous.
Each equipped with unique knowledge, experience, and background to review the document from an indigenous perspective.
Section D, quality of life, provides direction on how the city addresses the cultural and social identity and development of the community.
The subsection on heritage conservation provides direction on the identification on the identification of conservation and support for heritage properties and sites.
The objective is to identify and conserve Saskatoon's heritage resources and recognize their importance in telling the story of Saskatoon pre and post settlement.

Policy language supports the maintenance and use of a heritage plan and civic heritage policy, maintaining a listing of significant heritage resources in the city in the form of a publicly accessible registry.
Providing support and incentives for heritage property owners and identifying opportunities to conserve and honour indigenous culture and heritage.

Policy language also supports identifying opportunities for heritage conservation districts, creative use and programming to promote tourism and heritage resources and sites and protecting important ecosystems and natural heritage as part of the land development process.

Section E, environmental leadership, focuses on sustainability and the environment with policy supporting wetlands, conservation and natural areas like soils, riverbank stewardship and climate mitigation and adaptation.
This is largely a new addition to the OCP as there has been significant work focused on the environment to sustainability and recent years.
And by consolidating this direction, there is a clear framework to support this ongoing work and future-related work.
This section includes policies that address heritage.
The conservation of natural areas, subsections supports conserving and protecting natural features, maintaining an inventory of natural areas and assets and conserving archaeological sites.
These policies protect enhance and conserve important natural areas of the city in the city of region.

The riverbank stewardship subsection supports protecting and conserving the sites, Saskatchewan River Valley, monitoring areas of the riverbank prone to stomping or instability and establishing the riverbank slope overly district in the zoning by law.
Section G, sustainable growth guides house ascertain grows where new growth occurs and how neighborhoods should be designed.

The downtown and city center subsection includes policy, language on the protection of heritage properties and sites, support for programs and incentives, recognition of 21st Street as and its historic role in the downtown.
And protecting significant heritage buildings in the city center by encouraging their conservation, reuse and or conversion to residential uses.
Lastly, section J implementation provides direction for how the city will implement and achieve the OCP.

This includes a provision of policies regarding coordinating with with other jurisdictions indigenous inclusion and public engagement secondary plans and development phasing constraints to development zoning by the requirements subdivisions and operating capital budgeting policies in this section provide support for heritage through wording on architectural control districts.
These policies outline the requirements for designation and that the zoning by law is to contain specific guidelines for each architectural control district.
So with the approval of the OCP phase two of the project is underway.
The intent of this phase is to develop and implement a strategy to support the OCP's consistent use monitoring and maintenance.

This involves establishing communication and city departments and advisory committees and other stakeholders regarding relevant policy direction to ensure that the OCP continues to reflect the city's evolving direction.
Phase two will also establish a process for tracking work and decisions that may inspire future amendments.
